pages.title: Gangue
pages.text: Rock is not metal. What a lump of ore yields comes with the stony part that was never metal, and that part becomes slag sitting in your bath.$p$pRich ore is the cleanest at roughly 5-8% of the bath, normal 8-13%, poor 10-17%, and the small fragments you sweep off the ground 12-20%.

pages.title: You Cannot See It
pages.text: Nothing on the item tells you how dirty this particular lump is, and two lumps of the same grade differ a little from each other. The only honest reading is the Slag line in the crucible after they are in there.$p$pMelting refined metal instead brings its own history: flawed scrap keeps the slag it was cast with.

pages.title: So What
pages.text: Smelting straight from rock always gives Flawed metal, because the slag is over the 2% line before you have done anything wrong with the ratio.$p$pThere are two ways out of that. Lift the slag back out of the bath with a bowl and a flux, or take the dirt out of the rock before it ever goes near a fire.$p$pWashing is the cheaper habit once you have a barrel, and the only way to fill a crucible from a heap of poor ore without drowning it.

pages.title: Crushing Liberates Nothing
pages.text: The quern breaks a lump into grit: seven handfuls from a rich one, five from a normal, three from a poor, two out of the small fragments.$p$pEach handful melts to 5 mB of metal and carries the same share of stone as the lump it came from, so crushing on its own buys you **nothing** but the next step. It is the grinding that frees the grains of mineral from the rock so water can tell them apart.

pages.title: Washing Is the Paying Step
pages.text: Five handfuls of crushed ore pushed into a barrel of water come out as two of **concentrate**, worth 10 mB each - so four fifths of the metal survives and a fifth goes off in the tailings, which is what a hand jig actually does.$p$pWhat you lose in metal you buy back in dirt: a concentrate brings about **1.5%** of the bath as slag instead of the 7 to 19% the raw grades carry, which is inside what bronze will tolerate. Washed copper and washed tin can pour clean bronze with no skim at all.$p$pSteel is the exception, as always: it tolerates half of one percent, so even washed iron still wants flux and a bowl.

pages.title: Only the Heavy Minerals Wash
pages.text: Water sorts by weight, so it takes the ores whose mineral is far heavier than quartz: hematite, limonite and magnetite, cassiterite, malachite, and native copper, gold and silver.$p$pSphalerite, bismuthinite, tetrahedrite and garnierite are not much heavier than the rock they sit in, and no amount of washing will clean them - those you have to skim in the bath, or flux.
